title: The evening review
hookLine: a short honest look back at the day
tomorrow: one sage had a sentence he said going to bed. what was it?

cards: At closing time, a shop counts the till: what came in, what went out, what's missing. A Jewish moral teacher, Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, borrowed exactly that picture.
In his book The Path of the Just, he says a person should weigh their ways every day, the way merchants keep checking their accounts so nothing quietly goes wrong. So that's the merchant at the till.
The real question is what kind of counting he means.

teach.b: The practice has a name: cheshbon hanefesh, an accounting of the soul. Cheshbon is also the everyday Hebrew word for a bill. Luzzatto wasn't the first to use it.

An earlier teacher, Bahya ibn Paquda, gave a whole section of his book Duties of the Heart to it, and the Talmud, playing with a verse in Numbers, hears the town of Heshbon as a call: come, let's make an accounting.
Here's what makes the merchant picture work. A merchant doesn't count the till to feel terrible.

teach.h: FIND THE LEAK, NOT A VERDICT.
teach.b: He counts to find the leak, so tomorrow goes better. Nobody shuts the shop over one wrong coin; they notice it, fix the habit, and open again in the morning. That's the kindness inside the review.

teach.h: DON'T BE WICKED IN YOUR OWN EYES.
teach.b: Pirkei Avot guards the other side with a short line: don't be wicked in your own eyes. An honest count includes what went right, and then it ends.
So the evening review is brief: what came in today, what went out, where it leaked, what changes tomorrow. Then the book closes.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Hebrew for soul-searching shares its word with the check at a restaurant.

how: Some Jews keep a nightly cheshbon hanefesh, a few minutes of honest review before bed, sometimes in a small notebook; Musar study groups sometimes practice it together. It's also part of the run-up to the High Holy Days.

o: a short, fair look back at the day before sleep
a nightly prayer asking God to judge the day
a list of tomorrow's tasks made each night

games.q: the soul's account — tap the pairs.
p: a sum, or the check at a restaurant
weigh your ways daily, like a merchant
a town the Talmud hears as 'accounting'
don't be wicked in your own eyes

s: a Jewish evening review is about punishing yourself for the day
the merchant counts to find the leak, not to shut the shop; Avot says don't be wicked in your own eyes.
an earlier teacher, Bahya ibn Paquda, gave a whole section of a book to the soul's accounting
a good review goes over every minute until you've found everything wrong
it's brief: what came in, what went out, what changes tomorrow. then the book closes.

games.q: your roommate lies awake listing everything she got wrong this week. what would a cheshbon hanefesh look like for her?
o: keep going until the list is complete; honesty means no limits.
a short count: what went right, one leak, one change, then close the book.
skip it; looking back at mistakes only keeps people up.
games.why: Luzzatto's merchant checks the books to keep the business healthy, and Avot warns against being wicked in your own eyes. count, fix, close.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper, a receipt is perfect, and feel its edge between your fingers. Write two short lines by hand, listening to the pen move: one thing today that went right, and one thing you'd do differently tomorrow.
Read both once, the way a fair bookkeeper reads a ledger, then fold the paper in half and set it down. The day is counted.

wordCard.voice: The evening review: cheshbon hanefesh at the end of the day, a short and honest count, kept fair, then closed.

orig.note: Hebrew: an accounting of the soul; cheshbon is a sum, a bill or an account.

carryVoice: Your line: look back kindly. Count the day, find the leak, and let the ledger close for the night.

sources.ref: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, Mesillat Yesharim (The Path of the Just), chapter 3 (weigh one's ways daily, like merchants checking their accounts)
